```ts
export function limitFunction<Arguments extends unknown[], ReturnType>(
	function_: (...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType>,
```

- Input parameter type is `(...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType>`: a `PromiseLike` is required, unlike the `LimitFunction` call signature whose parameter type is `(...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType> | ReturnType` (plain return values allowed there). - The wrapper creates its own limiter internally (`const limit = pLimit(options);`), so it limits concurrent calls of that single function rather than across separate functions.

content.text:
Process an iterable of inputs with limited concurrency.

The mapper function receives the item value and its index.

Returns a promise equivalent to `Promise.all(Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)))`.

If the iterable throws during iteration, the returned promise rejects with that error. Mapper functions that were already scheduled still run, and their results are discarded.

This is a convenience function for processing inputs that arrive in batches. For more complex use cases, see [p-map](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-map).

### limit.activeCount

The number of promises that are currently running.

### limit.pendingCount

The number of promises that are waiting to run (i.e. their internal `fn` was not called yet).

### limit.clearQueue()

Discard pending promises that are waiting to run.

This might be useful if you want to tear down the queue at the end of your program's lifecycle or discard any function calls referencing an intermediary state of your app.

Note: This does not cancel promises that are already running.

When `rejectOnClear` is enabled, pending promises are rejected with an `AbortError`.
This is recommended if you await the returned promises, for example with `Promise.all`, so pending tasks do not remain unresolved after `clearQueue()`.

### limit.concurrency

Get or set the concurrency limit.

### limitFunction(fn, options) <sup>named export</sup>

Returns a function with limited concurrency.

The returned function manages its own concurrent executions, allowing you to call it multiple times without exceeding the specified concurrency limit.

Ideal for scenarios where you need to control the number of simultaneous executions of a single function, rather than managing concurrency across multiple functions.

Declaration as read in `index.d.ts` before this session's edits:

```ts
export function limitFunction<Arguments extends unknown[], ReturnType>(
	function_: (...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType>,
	options: Options
```

newMemories.name: limiter-active-slot-and-promise-settlement.md
newMemories.content:
---
name: limiter-active-slot-and-promise-settlement
description: p-limit reserves a concurrency slot at dequeue and resolves the caller promise with the job promise before it settles
type: project
---
How the p-limit limiter in `index.js` accounts for and settles work, as read from source:

- `resumeNext()` does `activeCount++;` and then `queue.dequeue().run();`, so a dequeued item occupies a concurrency slot from the moment it leaves the queue.
- `enqueue()` stores the internal `resolve` as `queueItem.run` and hands the job to `run` through `.then(run.bind(...))`, so a slot can be reserved while the job function itself has not been invoked yet.
- `pendingCount` is documented as "The number of promises that are waiting to run (i.e. their internal `fn` was not called yet)" and is backed by `queue.size`; a reserved, already-dequeued item is therefore counted in `activeCount`, not `pendingCount`.
- `run()` calls `resolve(result)` with `result = (async () => function_(...arguments_))()` before it `await result`, so the caller's promise adopts the job's eventual state while the slot stays occupied. `activeCount` is decremented only in `next()`, after the awaited result settles (a rejection is caught by `catch {}` and still reaches `next()`). Resolving with the job promise does not mean the job has completed.

Any idle-style predicate built on this bookkeeping has to treat a reserved slot as busy; the requested `onIdle` contract states this directly ("It resolves when both running/reserved slots and the waiting queue are empty.").

evidence.quote: The number of promises that are waiting to run (i.e. their internal `fn` was not called yet).
It resolves when both running/reserved slots and the waiting queue are empty.

newMemories.content:
---
name: node20-ava-domexception-test-skip
description: p-limit skips its AbortError clearQueue tests on Node 20; a source comment cites an AVA DOMException throwsAsync bug
type: project
---
In `test.js`, the tests that assert `clearQueue()` rejections are gated on the Node major version:

```js
// Node.js 20 has a bug where DOMException is not properly handled by AVA's `throwsAsync`.
const testClearQueueRejects = process.versions.node.startsWith('20.') ? test.skip : test;

testClearQueueRejects('clearQueue rejects pending promises when enabled', async t => {
```

`testClearQueueRejects('limitFunction exposes clearQueue', async t => {` uses the same gate, so on Node 20 both the limiter and the `limitFunction` wrapper AbortError assertions are skipped instead of run; elsewhere plain `test(...)` cases (for example the non-rejecting `'clearQueue'` test) still run.

The stated cause is that source comment about Node.js 20 and AVA's `throwsAsync` handling of `DOMException`; it is what the source says, not an independently verified defect. New regression tests for rejection behavior should keep this platform gate in mind rather than assuming those assertions execute on Node 20.
